workEn: The Secret History of the Mongols
title: 元朝秘史 §§131–135
titleEn: The Secret History of the Mongols — §§131–135: Belgütei's Wound, the Tatar Campaign, and Wang Qan
part: §§131–135 — Belgütei's Wound, the Tatar Campaign, and Wang Qan
source: Mongγol-un niγuča tobčiyan (The Secret History of the Mongols), §§131–135, in the Ming Chinese-character phonetic transcription, as edited with a romanized reading by Shiratori Kurakichi 白鳥庫吉, 音訳蒙文元朝秘史 (Tokyo, 1943), itself based on the Ye Dehui 葉德輝 printed edition of 1905/1908; text taken from the Japanese Wikisource transcription, archived and verified against it character for character. Shiratori died in 1942, so the edition was public domain in Japan before the URAA date and was never restored in the United States. Section numbering (§) is the standard citation system. Romanization convention: Shiratori's, kept exactly as he prints it (γ, ġ, ṅ, ž, č, and the raised dot of γ̇). Translations are made fresh from the Mongolian, with the Ming interlinear Chinese glosses as the primary crib. No modern translation was consulted. langCode is null: there is no text-to-speech for Middle Mongol.
about: Five sections. §131 tells of a feast at which a thief who took a rein-strap is seized, and Büri-Bökö, shielding the man, cuts Belgütei's bared shoulder with a sabre, and Belgütei asks his elder brother to hold back. §132 follows the Jurkin quarrel to its settlement and the Altan Qan's order to Wang-Jing Chancellor to drive the Tatars up the Ulja. §133 has Chinggis and To'oril join the Altan Qan's man, take the Tatar fort at Naratu-Shitügen and kill Megüjin-Se'ültü. §134 gives the titles (Ja'ud-quri, Wang) that follow. §135 brings home a small child found in the Tatar camp, whom Chinggis gives to his mother Högelün to bring up as her sixth son. The Mongol readings follow Shiratori throughout; the English is a first drafting, and several words rest on the Ming glosses alone.
draftNote: The Mongol readings follow Shiratori throughout; the English is a first drafting.

sentences.l: That feast us-from Belgütei having-arranged, Čiṅgis Qaγan's gelding holding standing was.
sentences.i: Belgütei, set to it from our side, stood holding Chinggis Qahan's geldings at that feast.
sentences.n: Tere qurim bidan-ača Belgütei žasaγ̇ad is the opening of the feast: bidan-ača (Ming 俺處) is 'from us, from our side', and žasaγ̇ad (Ming 整治) 'having arranged, set in order'. Whether Belgütei arranged the feast or arranged the horses is not clear from the Ming; I read 'set to it from our side'. Čiṅgis Qaγan-(n)u aγta barižu bain büleġe is 'holding the Qahan's geldings, was standing' (Ming 騸馬拿着立有來): barižu is the converb -žu, bain büleġe a progressive 'was standing'. Shiratori's stop closes the sentence.

sentences.t: Žürkin-eče Büri-Bökö tere qurim žasan büleġe.

morph.gloss: the Jurkin, a Mongol clan (clan name) [種(名)]
Büri-Bökö, a man's name (personal name; bökö 'wrestler, strongman') [人名]

sentences.l: Žürkin-from Büri-Bökö that feast arranging was.
sentences.i: On the Jurkin side, Büri-Bökö was managing that feast.
sentences.n: Žürkin-eče (Ming 種名行) is the clan name with the ablative -eče, 'from the Jurkin'. The Ming gloss is 行, which elsewhere marks a dative, but the parallel with bidan-ača in the line before makes it 'from the Jurkin side', as 'from our side' was. žasan is žasa- with the converb -n (Ming 整治), and žasan büleġe 'was arranging'. Büri-Bökö's name is Ming 人名 only; bökö is 'wrestler'.

sentences.i: A Qadagidai man seized the thief who had stolen a rein-strap from our dismounting-place.
sentences.n: bidan-u kilüġese-eče is 'from our dismounting-place' (Ming 下馬處, 'where one gets off the horse'), which I guess was where the horses were left at the feast; the stem kilüġese is not known to me, so only 'dismounting-place' (the Ming) is firm. qulaγuγsan-i qulaγai (Ming 偷了的行 賊) is 'the thief who had stolen', the participle -γsan with the accusative -i: the one seized is the thief. čilbür is a rein-strap (Ming 韁繩皮, 'rein-leather'). Qadagidai küġün is 'a Qadagidai man' (Ming 種名 人); who the clan is, the Ming does not say.

sentences.l: Büri-Bökö that man-own shielding, Belgütei as-usual in-grappling right sleeve-own having-pulled-off bare going was.
sentences.i: Büri-Bökö shielded that man of his, while Belgütei, who as always when grappling had pulled off his right sleeve, was going about bare-armed.
sentences.n: Büri-Bökö tere küġü-ben qoimasču: the thief is Büri-Bökö's man (küġü-ben, with the reflexive -ben, 'his own man'), and he is 'shielding' (Ming 護着). The stem of qoimasču is a guess from the Ming. Then Belgütei nasuda abaldurun: nasuda (Ming 如常) 'as usual', abaldurun (Ming 相搏) 'when grappling, wrestling', a stem abal- with a reciprocal; I read that Belgütei used to strip his sleeve to wrestle. baraγ̇un qanču-ban mültülžü is 'having pulled off his own right sleeve'; ničügün jabuqu büleġe (Ming 赤裸行有來) 'was going about bare'. Whether Büri-Bökö and Belgütei are one sentence or two, the Ming does not show; Shiratori has no stop until büleġe.

sentences.i: So Büri-Bökö slashed with a sabre at Belgütei's bared shoulder, splitting it open.

sentences.l: Belgütei thus being-cut being, what-to even not making, not coming(?), blood letting-trickle going-(acc.),
sentences.i: Belgütei, cut like that, made nothing of it, did not come at him, and went on, the blood running —
sentences.n: A long chain is broken here at Shiratori's lack of a stop: this unit is Belgütei, the next the Qahan who sees him. Note ülü (Ming 不), the negative that goes with present and converb forms (ülü bolγan, ülü jeṅgeren); keep an eye out for it against ese. čabčiγdažu is the passive čabči-γda- 'be cut', böġed 'being so, even so'. jaγ̇un-a ba ülü bolγan is 'making it into nothing at all' (Ming 甚麽也不做). The doubtful word is jeṅgeren: the Ming gives only 來, 'come', and with ülü I read 'not coming (at him)', that is, not hitting back; 'not flinching' is possible. I cannot say. čisun čuburiγ̇ulžu is 'making the blood trickle' (Ming 敎溜着, the causative -γ̇ul-), and jabuqui-ji is a participle with the accusative -ji: it is the object of 'seeing' in the next unit.

sentences.t: Čiṅgis Qaγan seġüder-tür saγ̇užu qurim dotorāča üžežü γarču irežü ügülerün:

morph.gloss: Chinggis, a man's name (the title taken by Temüjin in 1206) [太祖︀]

sentences.l: Čiṅgis Qaγan shade-in sitting, feast inside-from seeing, going-out coming, on-speaking:
sentences.i: Chinggis Qahan, who was sitting in the shade, saw him from inside the feast, came out, and said:
sentences.n: Čiṅgis Qaγan seġüder-tür saγ̇užu: seġüder (Ming 影) is 'shade, shadow', here the shade of a tent or tree (as I read it) where the Qahan sat. dotorāča is 'from inside', with a long vowel where the stem vowel and the ablative -ača run together (Ming 裏處). The converbs üžežü 'seeing', γarču 'going out', irežü 'coming' chain the Qahan's acts; the object seen is the man of the last unit, jabuqui-ji.

sentences.t: "Ker ein kigden büleġe bida"

morph.gloss: we, us (inclusive: you and I; first-person plural pronoun) [咱]

sentences.l: "How thus being-made was we"
sentences.i: "How have we been treated so?"
sentences.n: Ker ein kigden büleġe bida: kigden is ki- 'do, make' with the passive -gde- and the converb -n (Ming 被做, 'being made'), büleġe the past 'was', so 'how have we come to be done thus?'. Whether it means 'treated' (as in i) or 'made to do' I cannot tell from the Ming. Shiratori's opening mark is on Ker and the closing one on bida.

sentences.t: kēküi-dür Belgütei ügülerün:"

morph.gloss: Belgütei, a man's name (personal name) [人名]

sentences.l: on-saying Belgütei on-speaking:
sentences.i: At this Belgütei said:
sentences.n: kēküi-dür is keġe- 'say' with the participle -küi and the dative-locative -dür, 'at the saying' (Ming 說時), the two e's written long. It looks back to the Qahan's question; the pair of verbs is 'when he said (that), Belgütei spoke'. Shiratori's mark opens the speech after the colon.

sentences.t: Mer üdüġüi büleġe.

morph.gloss: wound, injury (stem read from the Ming 傷) [傷]

sentences.l: Wound not-yet was.
sentences.i: "It is not yet a wound."
sentences.n: Mer üdüġüi büleġe is hard: the Ming reads 傷未有來, 'wound / not yet / was'. mer I take as 'wound, hurt' (Ming 傷), üdüġüi as 'not yet'. I read it as Belgütei brushing the cut off, 'it is not yet a wound'; 'I am not yet hurt' would do as well. The sense is uncertain and the next speech does not decide it.

sentences.t: min-u tula aqa deġü-dür maγ̇uγalin bolulčaγ̇užai.

sentences.l: My because-of, elder-brother younger-brother-to reproaching-each-other lest-it-become.
sentences.i: "On my account it might come to a falling-out between brother and brother.
sentences.n: min-u tula is 'because of me' (Ming 我的上頭). aqa deġü-dür (Ming 兄弟行) is 'to elder brother, to younger brother', that is, between the two; the Ming 行 marks the dative on the second. maγ̇uγalin (Ming 相怪, 'blame one another') seems to be from maγ̇u 'bad', but the split of the word is a guess. bolulčaγ̇užai is bol- 'become' with -γ̇užai, an apprehensive ending (Ming 恐, 'I fear that'), 'lest it become'; the middle -ulča- is uncertain.

sentences.t: Bi ülü alžaqu; bi ilaγ̇ari bijü.

morph.gloss: to hinder, be in the way (stem inferred from the Ming 礙事) [礙事]
to excel, be better (stem inferred from the Ming 較好) [較好]

sentences.l: I not hindering; I better am.
sentences.i: It is no hindrance to me; I am the better man."
sentences.n: Bi ülü alžaqu: alžaqu I take as alža- 'hinder, be in the way' (Ming 礙事) with the participle -qu: 'it does not hinder me', 'it is nothing to me'. Bi ilaγ̇ari bijü: ilaγ̇ari (Ming 較好, 'rather good') is probably from ilaγ̇a- 'excel, be better'; the ending is unclear. bijü is the present of bü- 'to be'. Whether he says 'I am the better' (stronger) or 'I am all right' is not settled by the Ming; i takes the first, which fits a man who could win and will not.

sentences.t: Aqa deġü-dür sai ižilidülčen büküi-dür aqa bütügei; qorumud bai" keġebe.

morph.gloss: just now, only now (read from the Ming 恰纔; not the usual sai 'good') [恰纔]
to become used to (stem inferred from the Ming 慣熟) [慣熟]
let it not be, do not (prohibitive) [休]

sentences.l: Elder-brother younger-brother-to just-now getting-used-to-each-other being-when, elder-brother do-not; for-a-while stay" he-said.
sentences.i: "While brother and brother are only just growing used to each other, elder brother, do not. Stay a while," he said.
sentences.n: The sense I have is Belgütei's plea to Chinggis ('elder brother', the second aqa, Ming (兄)) to hold back. sai (Ming 恰纔) is taken as 'just now, only just', not the usual sai 'good'. ižilidülčen (Ming 慣熟, 'used to each other') has a stem ižili- 'become used to' (guessed from the Ming), a reciprocal -dül- and an ending -čen that I cannot identify. büküi-dür is 'when being' (Ming 有時). bütügei is the prohibitive 'let it not be, do not' (Ming 休), and the thing not to be done is not named. qorumud (Ming 且) is 'for a while, meanwhile' with a final -d I cannot explain; bai is the bare imperative 'stay!'.

sentences.l: Čiṅgis Qaγan, Belgütei, those, if-urging, not becoming,
sentences.i: When Chinggis Qahan and Belgütei urged those men, it came to nothing;
sentences.n: This opening is doubtful. Čiṅgis Qaγan Belgütei tedüi is 'Chinggis Qahan, Belgütei, those (men)' (Ming 那些), tedüi taken as the pronoun 'those' and not the adverb 'so'. idqaγ̇asu (Ming 勸呵) is idqa- 'urge, persuade' (stem guessed) with the conditional -γ̇asu (Ming 呵, 'if, when'). ülü bolun 'not becoming' I read as 'it not working, not being persuaded'. Who is persuaded, and by whom, is not clear; the next unit shows Chinggis's side breaking off branches, so the Jurkin would not be persuaded.

sentences.l: tree's branches snapping-off pulling-together, leather-tub's churn-poles pulling-out taking,
sentences.i: they snapped off branches from the trees, tore out the churning-poles from the leather tub, and took them,
sentences.n: modun-u gešiġüd (Ming 木的枝每) is 'the branches of the tree', the plural -d. quγuru tatalažu (Ming 折扯着) is 'snapping off and pulling'; the -la- is unclear (the Ming 扯着 gives only 'pulling'), so I read the pair as 'snapping off and pulling'. itügesün büleġüd (Ming 皮桶的撞馬乳椎) is 'the churn-poles of the leather tub': büleġüd is the plural of a word for the plunger used to beat mare's milk, not the verb büleġe 'was'. itügesün is unknown to me; I read it as 'leather vat'. suγučižu abču (Ming 抽出着要着) 'pulling out, taking'. The subject is not named; it is Chinggis's side.

sentences.n: ašigilaldužu (Ming 厮打着, 'fighting one another') is ašigi- 'beat' with -la- and the reciprocal -ldu-. Žürkin-i ilaγču (Ming 人名行勝着) is 'beating the Jurkin'. žirin-i is the numeral 'two (persons)' with the accusative, and sums up the two named before it. buližu abuba (Ming 奪着要了) 'snatching, took'. In i I give Qatun as part of the name.

sentences.t: Žiči müd žokilduja keġegdežü

morph.gloss: they (third-person plural pronoun; the exact form is uncertain) [他每]
to be fitting, agree (stem inferred from the Ming 和) [商和咱]

sentences.l: But they "let-us-settle" being-said,
sentences.i: But when they were told, "Let us come to terms,"
sentences.n: žokilduja (Ming 商和咱) is a hortative: žoki- 'be fitting, agree' (stem guessed from the Ming 和) with the reciprocal -ldu- and the first-person -ja, 'let us come to an agreement'. keġegdežü is keġe- 'say' with the passive -gde-: 'being told'. müd (Ming 他每) is 'they'. Who says it to whom, Shiratori does not show; I read that the Jurkin proposed terms.

sentences.i: the two ladies, Qorijin Qatun and Qughurchin Qatun, were sent back, with the words, "Let us come to terms,"
sentences.n: ičuγ̇ažu is the causative of ič- 'withdraw' (Ming 退着) with -uγ̇a-: 'making retire, sending back'. The commas are Shiratori's. The subject is Chinggis's side, handing the women back (a guess from the context, the Ming does not name it); i uses the passive so as not to name the sender, since the previous unit's 'they' is the other party.

sentences.i: While envoys were going to and fro, the Altan Qan of the Khitan people, when Megüjin-Se'ültü and the other Tatars were not coming into counsel with him, to Wang-Jing Chancellor:
sentences.n: The hardest line of the part. elčileldün büküi-dür (Ming 使臣往來有的時) is 'while envoys go back and forth'. Kitad irgen-ü Altan Qān is the Altan (Jin) Qan, 'of the Khitan people' (Ming 契丹百姓的金皇帝). Megüžin-Seġültü-ten, with -ten 'and those', is Megüžin-Seġültü and his company. eje-dür(i)-jen (Ming 商量自的行, 'in their own consulting') has a stem eje I cannot identify, and ülü oroγdarun (Ming 不見入) is oro- 'enter' with a passive: 'not being let in'. The reflexive -(i)jen, 'own', would then point back to the Altan Qan: his own counsel. I read that the Tatars would not enter into talks. The Ming gives 'not seen entering'. This is guesswork. Waṅgiṅ-Žaṅsijaṅ-a is dative: 'to Wang-Jing Chancellor', and the speech follows.
